The Great Transatlantic Pact: Unpacking the EU–Mercosur Agreement
An in-depth analysis of the most ambitious trade agreement between Europe and South America, its geopolitical implications and the tensions surrounding it.
18 March 2026 · Politics
«Commerce is the great civilising agent»
— Juan Bautista Alberdi. Bases and Points of Departure for the Political Organisation of the Argentine Republic (1852).

On 6 December 2024, after twenty years of intermittent negotiations, the European Union and Mercosur signed what Brussels proclaims as "the largest free trade area ever created by the EU". Formally approved by the European Council in January 2026, the EU–Mercosur Partnership Agreement (EMPA) promises to unite 720 million consumers and unlock bilateral trade worth €111 billion a year.

The agreement must still be ratified by the European Parliament. But behind the headline figures and the triumphalist announcements lies a complex matrix of calculated concessions, disguised protections and compromises that reveal both the aspirations and the deep fears of the two blocs. This is not a simple free trade agreement; it is a reflection of the geopolitical realities of the twenty-first century: the tension between commercial openness and economic sovereignty, between climate ambitions and industrial competitiveness, between European regulatory soft power and South American comparative advantage.

What is most interesting, though, emerges when we set aside the narrow commercial lens and focus instead on the historical impact of the EU's trade agreements with other countries — on the volume and number of foreign direct investments in the signatory area or countries, which saw a significant increase.
The Agricultural Dilemma

The principal cause of the long stalemate in negotiations has always been the agri-food sector. European producers, particularly in France, Ireland and Poland, feared an avalanche of cheap South American meat. Mercosur governments dreamed of significant access to the lucrative European market. The reality set out in the agreement is more nuanced: managed access, not full liberalisation.

The compromise reached is an exercise in surgical precision. The EU grants a new quota of 99,000 tonnes of beef at a preferential tariff of 7.5%, far below the MFN tariff of 60-74%. Added to the existing modified quotas, total preferential access reaches 162,000 tonnes.

Contextual analysis, however, reveals European caution: this volume represents only 1.5% of total EU production. Brussels is willing to offer an orderly, regulated channel, but not open competition that would threaten its livestock farmers.

More important than the quotas may be a pre-existing regulation: the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR), in force since December 2024. This requirement demands full traceability and certification that products such as beef, soya and coffee do not come from land deforested after 2020.

This non-tariff mechanism acts as a powerful filter. It classifies countries such as Brazil and Paraguay as "high risk", subject to intensive inspection. Uruguay, with its cattle traceability system operating since 2006, benefits as a "low risk" supplier. In this way the EU uses its regulatory power to externalise its environmental standards, converting a potential trade barrier into a condition of market access. For years now the green agenda has become a para-tariff instrument widely used by the European Union.

The wine sector is one of the clearest winners in terms of brand positioning and market access. Under the agreement, the EU will eliminate tariffs on Mercosur wines (currently between €13 and €32 per hectolitre) immediately for bottled premium products, while bulk wines will see a gradual phase-out over up to 8 years.

Mercosur honey gains access to a 45,000-tonne quota at a 0% tariff, which will strengthen beekeeping cooperatives against competition from honey from other markets. In fisheries, the elimination of tariffs (reaching 25% for hake fillets or prawns) will energise the ports of the South Atlantic, although the agreement imposes strict rules of origin.

The ethanol sector, Brazil's in particular, stands to gain substantially. Two quotas are granted totalling 650,000 tonnes (some 823 million litres). The Brazilian advantage is twofold: its sugar cane ethanol has a carbon footprint 70% lower than American maize ethanol or European beet ethanol, aligning perfectly with the European Green Deal.
Mercosur's industrial protection
If Europe protected its agriculture, Mercosur did the same for its industrial base, especially the automotive sector, emblematic for Brazil and Argentina.

The agreement does not eliminate overnight the tariff that today stands at 35%. It establishes a 15-year transition period for combustion vehicles, with a non-linear structure designed for a soft landing:
Years 1–7 (Grace Phase)
Only 50,000 units a year enter at a tariff halved to 17.5%. The rest pay the full 35%.
Years 8–15 (Accelerated Phase-out)
The tariff begins to fall more sharply until reaching 0% in 2041.
For hybrid vehicles (PHEV), protection lasts even longer: 30 years (until 2056), and 18 years in the electric case.

Mercosur negotiated a specific sectoral safeguard mechanism (Annex 9-A) with lower activation thresholds. While the general safeguard requires "serious injury", the automotive one requires only a demonstration of "injury". A rise in sectoral unemployment above 8% (against 10% generally) could justify the temporary reintroduction of tariffs of up to 25%.
Dispute settlement and export taxes

The Mercosur–EU agreement has managed to impose its Investment Court System (ICS) model. The Investor-State Dispute Settlement (ISDS) mechanism operates through a permanent court with judges designated in advance by both parties, with transparency objectives and an appeal system, while protecting through safeguards the states' "right to regulate" in areas such as public health, the environment and security.

The question of export taxes is another interesting aspect. The EU–Mercosur agreement establishes a clear rule: Mercosur countries may not create new export duties nor increase existing ones on products they sell to the EU. This means that Argentina, which today levies export taxes of 33% on soya, 15% on beef and 12% on wheat, is left with those rates as a maximum ceiling — it may maintain or lower them, but not raise them.

The logic behind this clause is simple: the EU does not want to eliminate its tariffs only for Argentina to raise its export taxes and capture that benefit through internal taxation. In other words, the agreement seeks to ensure that tariff preferences actually reach producers and make Mercosur products more competitive in Europe, rather than allowing the state to appropriate them through export levies.
The Impact of Investment Treaties with the EU: Lessons from Mexico, Chile and South Korea

As Mercosur prepares to implement its historic agreement with the European Union, the precedents of countries that have already travelled this road offer valuable lessons and, in some cases, clear warnings. The experiences of Mexico (with the EU-Mexico FTA), Chile (Association Agreement) and South Korea (EU-Korea FTA) show how investment agreements with Brussels can transform economies, but also generate unforeseen tensions and challenges.

When Mexico signed the Free Trade Agreement with the European Union (TLCUEM) in 2000, EU FDI in Mexico multiplied fivefold between 2000 and 2022, rising from approximately €10 billion to more than €50 billion. The automotive and aerospace sectors were the major beneficiaries.

The EU–Chile Association Agreement (2003) led EU FDI in Chile to double in the decade after the agreement, concentrated in renewable energy, sustainable mining and financial services. That FDI, however, concentrated on exploiting static comparative advantages (copper, lithium, fruit), with less than 15% going to high value-added manufacturing.

Finally, the EU–Korea FTA (2011) led European FDI in South Korea to triple in 5 years, mainly through strategic mergers and acquisitions and R&D investment, with joint centres in areas such as 5G and batteries.
Conclusion: An Agreement of Its Time, with Eyes on the Future

The EU–Mercosur agreement is a profoundly realistic document. It is not the triumph of orthodox free trade but the crystallisation of managed trade and of an investment opportunity. For the EU, the agreement secures agricultural and energy raw materials (ethanol, vegetable oils) for its green transition, opens protected markets for its high-value industries (machinery, pharmaceuticals, wines), exports its regulatory model and creates a secure, modern framework for its capital to finance investment in Mercosur.

For Mercosur, the agreement guarantees predictable if limited access to a high-purchasing-power market, attracts European investment and technology under more balanced rules — learning from the mistakes of past agreements — grants time for its industries to adapt and, critically, provides a platform for international integration that goes beyond selling commodities, betting on becoming a supplier of green solutions (biofuels, renewable energy) for Europe.

It also helps to address one of the biggest problems Mercosur has had since its founding: moving from being a navel-gazing trade agreement focused on the internal market to the opportunity to build on the success of this deal to advance others, such as those with Canada or South Korea.

Ultimately, the agreement is less a commercial revolution than a pact of stability and geo-economic reorientation. In a world fragmented by tensions between the United States and China, Europe and South America have chosen to anchor their relations in a framework of shared rules. The EU–Mercosur agreement arrives at a moment of reconfiguration of global value chains. The experience of Mexico, Chile and South Korea indicates that the final outcome will depend not only on the text of the treaty but on the capacity of Mercosur's governments and private sector to use this framework as a strategic lever for development rather than as a simple magnet for capital.
